analysis.title: US CPI: The Fed isn't done yet
key_insights: October CPI slowed to 0.4% MoM headline from 0.6% in September but beat the 0.3% expectation. Core CPI rose 0.3% MoM for the third month in a row, above the 0.2% consensus.

Energy CPI rose 0.7% MoM, down from 5.2% in September. Gasoline rose 1.0% after a 9.1% September surge, and fuel oil inflation slowed from 15.3% to 2.0% MoM. Food inflation accelerated to 0.5% from zero, with grocery and restaurant prices both rising.

Shelter inflation eased to 0.3% from 0.4% MoM but still accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase. Rent of primary residence rose 0.2%, owners' equivalent rent 0.3%, and lodging inflation moderated to 0.6% from 2.0%.

TS Lombard says the Fed has already begun tightening and the debate is how far rates need to rise. It expects a 25bp hike in December, based on recovering labour demand and renewed domestic inflation pressure that should outlast the energy shock.
The bank expects 25bp hikes once a quarter, with risks to the terminal rate skewed higher. Gradual tightening could ultimately produce a higher terminal rate than faster hikes would.

Waller said this morning that a 0.3% core CPI print would make a 50bp December hike necessary for 'credibility'. TS Lombard discounts the comment, saying Waller has not been a good guide to policy since Warsh took over, and says monthly CPI is noisy.

October payrolls rose 165k, with the recovery spanning manufacturing and services. Wage growth has turned higher outside education and healthcare, and faster pay on job-to-job moves suggests the broader market could follow.

Wage growth appears to be bottoming while measured productivity growth risks deteriorating as the labour market recovers. That points to renewed unit labour cost pressure, which firms may absorb through narrower margins or pass into consumer prices.
Aggregate profit growth could become less favourable as labour demand recovers, which the bank says threatens the broadening of profits it sees as central to sustaining the expansion.
Financial conditions have tightened but remain far from tight. Higher bond yields have begun to restrain AI investment, but there is little evidence of a broader monetary squeeze.

The AI investment boom and broadening economic activity should let the Fed keep tightening well beyond its initial response to energy inflation. Reacceleration in new hiring is bringing renewed capacity pressure back into focus.

Structural view on core services: wage growth is more responsive to domestic labour conditions, the retiring generation is larger than the one entering the workforce, and core services inflation is expected to average higher than in the post-GFC cycle.

Structural view on core goods: tariffs have pushed core goods inflation up and the energy shock adds pressure. De-globalisation and supply chain shifts should keep core goods inflation higher than in the 2010s. The Manheim used vehicle index has flipped down again.

Energy and food outlook: the report says temporary energy relief has evaporated and oil prices are swinging, though futures still point down. Food prices are gaining traction on margin expansion and second-round effects.

tension_points.bull_case: Waller says a 0.3% core CPI print would make a 50bp December hike necessary for credibility, which implies faster tightening.
tension_points.bear_case: TS Lombard argues the Fed has little reason to accelerate every meeting and expects 25bp quarterly hikes. Financial conditions are tighter but far from tight, and monthly CPI is noisy.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A further acceleration in new hiring and wage growth would push the terminal rate higher. Weaker labour demand would undermine the case for further hikes.

theme_stances.key_argument: Recovering labour demand and renewed domestic inflation pressure should outlast the energy shock, supporting further hikes.
Wage growth is bottoming while productivity risks deteriorating, pointing to renewed unit labour cost pressure.
